Random singlet physics in the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCu2F7

Abstract

We report a random singlet ground state in the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCu2F7. Cationic Na+/Cd2+ disorder on the pyrochlore AA site generates a broad distribution of Cu2+–F-–Cu2+ exchange couplings, introducing intrinsic magnetic bond disorder. Despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions (θCW=−72\theta_{\mathrm{CW}}=-72 K), no magnetic order or global spin freezing is observed in DC and AC susceptibility, specific heat or 23Na nuclear magnetic resonance to 120 mK, with muon spin relaxation experiments confirming persistent spin dynamics to 58 mK. TT-linear specific heat, a Curie-like susceptibility tail, and power-law scaling with data collapse in χ⁡(T)\chi(T), M⁡(H)M(H), Cmag/TC_{\mathrm{mag}}/T, 23Na (1/T1​T)(1/T_{1}T) and the muon spin polarization P⁡(t)P(t) reveal a disorder-driven network of random singlets and orphan spins. Scaling across multiple bulk and local probes is consistent with a broad distribution of exchange energies, P⁡[𝒥]∼𝒥−αP[\mathcal{J}]\sim\mathcal{J}^{-\alpha}. This behavior contrasts with previously-studied NaA′′​B2A^{\prime\prime}B_{2}F7 pyrochlore fluorides, where magnetic bond disorder precipitates spin-glass freezing, underscoring the crucial role of strong S=12S=\frac{1}{2} quantum fluctuations in NaCdCu2F7.

I Introduction

Quantum spin liquids (QSL) – highly entangled dynamic ground states without long-range magnetic order down to T=0T=0 – remain a central focus of frustrated magnetism due to their exotic fractionalized excitations and non-trivial topology [5, 73, 96, 46], with possible applications in quantum technologies [39, 58, 93, 83]. The S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the pyrochlore lattice is a canonical model [9]: corner-sharing tetrahedra produce strong geometrical frustration, suppressing semiclassical order and promoting competing ground states, with theoretical predictions spanning chiral or dimerized phases and QSLs with short-range correlations [23, 74, 20, 36, 84, 4, 75, 10].

Experimental realizations of ideal S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnets are exceedingly rare. Multiple rare-earth Jeff=12J_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{1}{2} pyrochlore oxides show QSL-like behaviour but suffer from strong anisotropy due to spin-orbit coupling and crystal field effects [18, 57, 81], whilst Jeff=12J_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{1}{2} Co2+-based pyrochlore fluorides freeze into glassy states due to magnetic bond disorder [28, 41, 42]. Lu2Mo2O5N2 [11] and Hg2Cu2F6S [30] represent the only known realizations of true S=12S=\frac{1}{2} pyrochlores. Lu2Mo2O5N2 exhibits a dynamic, QSL-like ground state without spin freezing despite significant disorder, in stark contrast to its spin-glass S=1S=1 counterpart Lu2Mo2O7, underscoring the role of strong S=12S=\frac{1}{2} quantum fluctuations. Hg2Cu2F6S also displays QSL-like behavior, but the lack of comprehensive low-temperature characterization leaves its ground-state nature unresolved.

In real materials, quenched disorder via site mixing, vacancies, or lattice distortions is unavoidable and can instead stabilize disorder-driven phases [67]. One prominent outcome is the random singlet (RS) state [88, 86, 87, 85, 32, 31, 91, 70, 51, 72, 79], where a broad distribution of antiferromagnetic (AF) exchange energies produces localized singlets over multiple length scales, while weakly coupled moments form paramagnetic “orphan spins”. The RS state can be distinguished from valence-bond solids (VBS) [27] and resonating valence-bond (RVB) manifolds [2] by its disorder-induced power-law distributions of exchange couplings P⁡[𝒥]∼𝒥−αP[\mathcal{J}]\sim\mathcal{J}^{-\alpha} and density of states ρ⁡(E)∼E−α\rho(E)\sim E^{-\alpha}, leading to a characteristic TT-linear specific heat, gapless susceptibility with a Curie-like tail, broad features in the dynamic spin structure factor, and power-law scaling of χ⁡(T)\chi(T), M⁡(H)M(H), and Cmag/TC_{\rm mag}/T with data collapse as a function of temperature and magnetic field T/HT/H [38, 37, 14, 17, 6]. RS behavior has been documented in 1D chains [90, 80, 35], 2D layered lattices [45, 40, 47, 77, 37, 82, 95, 55, 56, 49, 62, 54, 16], and a few 3D frustrated magnets [26, 68], but has not been established in a S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnet.

In this work, we provide conclusive evidence for a RS ground state in NaCdCu2F7, making it the first S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore where the RS state is confirmed across multiple probes. The inherent structural Na+/Cd2+ cationic disorder induces randomness in the Cu2+-F--Cu2+ magnetic superexchange pathways, forming the necessary distribution of exchange energies 𝒥\mathcal{J}. Despite the strong AF interactions (θCW=−72\theta_{\mathrm{CW}}=-72 K), no magnetic transition or global spin freezing is seen in DC magnetization, AC susceptibility, specific heat or 23Na nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and we confirm continued dynamics down to 58 mK via zero field (ZF) and longitudinal field (LF) muon spin relaxation (μ\muSR) measurements. Convincingly, evidence of power-law scaling and data collapse can be found in each of these experimental probes. The strong quantum fluctuations of the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Cu2+ ions suppress the spin-glass freezing observed in related pyrochlore fluoride materials [28, 29, 41, 42, 43, 69], instead giving rise to a RS state. This establishes NaCdCu2F7 as a benchmark platform for testing theoretical predictions of 3D random singlet physics and exploring low-energy excitations, field-tuned phenomena, and exotic quantum spin-liquid behavior in three dimensions.

II Experimental methods

NaCdCu2F7 was synthesized using the optical floating-zone method by melting a stoichiometric fluoride mix in a hollow graphite crucible, yielding a largely polycrystalline rod. Phase purity was verified by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD). Upon crushing the as-grown rod, small crystallites were isolated and used for structure solution using single crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD).

SCXRD was measured at 300 K using a Rigaku Xcalibur Gemini ultra-diffractometer, with graphite-monochromated Mo Kα\alpha (λ\lambda = 0.71073 Å) radiation, and an Atlas S2 CCD detector. Diffraction data were integrated using CrysAlis Pro [60] with an analytical numeric absorption correction combined with a multifaceted crystal model and an empirical absorption correction using spherical harmonics. The structure was solved by charge flipping using Superflip [63] and refined by full-matrix least squares in Jana2020 [64]. Structural graphics were created using Vesta [52].

DC magnetization measurements on powdered NaCdCu2F7 were performed in a Quantum Design Magnetic Property Measurement System (model MPMS-XL 7 T), in the temperature range T=−300T=1.8\!-\!300 K and the magnetic field range μ0​H=−7\mu_{0}H=0\!-\!7 T, using the reciprocating sample option (RSO).

High-field isothermal magnetization was measured in the High Magnetic Field Laboratory (Hochfeld-Magnetlabor Dresden, HLD) in the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) in Dresden, Germany, using a pulsed 60 T magnet with a cryostat setup allowing the temperature range T=−50T=1.35\!-\!50 K.

AC susceptibility was measured in the frequency range νAC=−10 000\nu_{\rm AC}=215\!-\!10\penalty\ 000 Hz between T=−4T=0.4\!-\!4 K, using a custom-made coil for the 3He option in a Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS).

Specific heat measurements were performed via the heat relaxation method in the PPMS between T=−300T=1.8\!-\!300 K, with the addition of a 3He low-temperature insert for temperatures T=−20T=0.4\!-\!20 K, in fields of μ0​H=−9\mu_{0}H=0\!-\!9 T. The lattice specific heat was removed by subtracting the specific heat of the non-magnetic analogue NaCdZn2F7 from the total specific heat. [28, 29] An Oxford Instruments Triton dilution refrigerator (DR) was employed for zero-field and in-field heat capacity measurements between T=−650T=150\!-\!650 mK.

ZF-μ\muSR and LF-μ\muSR measurements were performed at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory in Harwell Oxford, United Kingdom. [13] The MuSR instrument was used, utilising a dilution refrigerator cryostat setup for temperatures between T=−4T=0.05\!-\!4 K, allowing applied longitudinal fields between μ0​HLF=−3000\mu_{0}H_{\rm LF}=0\!-\!3000 G. The obtained spectra were analyzed using WiMDA [66] and Mantid [3].

NMR measurements were performed using a phase-coherent pulsed spectrometer with a superconducting NMR magnet. A 4He variable temperature insert (VTI) was utilized between T=−150T=1.8\!-\!150 K, and a 3He-4He dilution-refrigerator probe head was used between T=−2.1T=0.12\!-\!2.1 K. A custom-wound excitation coil from silver wire was used. Frequency-swept spectra at different constant fields were collected, with the radio-frequency (r.f.) circuit tuned and matched at each point. Nuclear spin echoes were generated using a standard 90°\degree–180°\degree pulse sequence, with a first-pulse duration of 2 - 3 μ\mus, where the r.f. power for nuclear spin excitation was optimized at each NMR spectral peak. The separation τ\tau between the first and second pulse was typically 20 - 30 μ\mus. Echoes were accumulated and Fourier transformed to obtain the spectra.

Details of the synthesis process, extended measurement details, and additional results of powder and single crystal X-ray difraction, magnetization, AC susceptibility, heat capacity, 23Na NMR, and μ\muSR measurements can be found in the Supplementary Material (SM) [1].

III Results

III.1 Structural details

Structural studies confirmed the expected cubic pyrochlore structure (space group F​d​3¯​mFd\overline{3}m, aa = 10.3038(15) Å) for NaCdCu2F7, depicted in Figure 1a, agreeing with the previously studied NaA′′​B2A^{\prime\prime}B_{2}F7 fluorides [22, 28, 29, 41, 42, 43, 69, 44, 59, 19]. Structural randomness is inherent due to a mixed occupancy of Na+/Cd2+ cations fully disordered on the pyrochlore (16​d16d) AA site. Inspection of the reciprocal space map cuts along the (h​k​0),(h​0​l)(hk0),(h0l) and (0​k​l)(0kl) planes reveals no superstructure reflections or obvious diffuse scattering, indicating the absence of short- or long-range occupational ordering of Na+ and Cd2+ (see Figure S2 in SM [1]). The magnetic Cu2+ ions on the pyrochlore (16​c16c) BB site are octahedrally coordinated by F(2) fluorine on the 48​f48f site, and are surrounded by six Na+/Cd2+ ions creating a hexagon in the (111) plane, see Figure 1b. The difference in ionic radii of Na+ (1.18 Å) and Cd2+ (1.10 Å) [76], in combination with their random occupation of the AA site, induce small trigonal distortions of the CuF6 octahedra along the local [111] direction, which leads to a distribution of Cu2+–F-–Cu2+ superexchange pathways - intrinsic magnetic bond disorder. The only free coordinate in the pyrochlore F​d​3¯​mFd\overline{3}m space group, the F(2) fluorine xx-coordinate xF⁡(2)x_{\rm F(2)}, dictates the size of the distortion of the CuF6 octahedron as well as the (Na/Cd)F8 dodecahedron. [28] The refined value, xF⁡(2)=0.3316​(4)x_{\rm F(2)}=0.3316(4), results in a deformed CuF6 octahedron with six equal Cu-F(2) bond lengths dCu−F⁡(2)=2.0060​(17)d_{\rm Cu-F(2)}=2.0060(17) Å, while the F(2)-Cu-F(2) angle deviates from the ideal 90°\degree value by ±δ=7.22​(10)​°\pm\delta=7.22(10)\degree.

Refinement of the Cd occupancy, constrained with the Na occupancy by occ(Na)+occ(Cd) = 1, lead to a better solution than the ideal stoichiometric 0.5/0.5 case. A small Cd deficiency of occ(Cd) = 0.462(4) was obtained. To preserve charge balance, a refinement of the F(2) occupancy as a function of the Cd occupancy was attempted in the form of Na1+xCd1-xCu2F7-x, leading to occ(F2) = 0.924(7) with slightly better residue values, giving the final refined composition Na1.076Cd0.924Cu2F6.924. However, this sligtly off-stoichiometric structure does neither change the bond lengths (see Figure S4 in SM [1]), nor the angles defining the CuF6 and (Na/Cd)F8 polyhedra, within the 3σ\sigma limit.

Atomic positions and thermal displacement parameters are summarized in Table 1 and 2. Detailed SCXRD structure solution results and additional details of the refinement process can be found in SM [1].

III.2 Magnetic properties

Temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility, χ⁡(T)=M⁡(T)/H\chi(T)=M(T)/H, shows no magnetic transition down to 1.8 K, seen in Figure 2a. Instead a diverging Curie-like tail is noted below 10 K, a typical sign of paramagnetic “orphan” spins dominating the low-temperature bulk magnetic properties. The orphan spin response, norp∼15%n_{\rm orp}\sim 15\% was identified and subtracted by fitting the isothermal magnetization M⁡(H)M(H) at 1.8 K (see detailed analysis below), resulting in the intrinsic susceptibility, χint=χ−χorp\chi_{\rm int}=\chi-\chi_{\rm orp}, also shown in Figure 2a. The χint\chi_{\rm int} displays a broad maximum centered around 3 K. A Curie-Weiss fit of the inverse total susceptibility χ−1​(T)\chi^{-1}(T) between 200–300 K, shown in Figure 2b, gives CC = 0.486(1) emu K mol-1 Oe-1 and θCW=−72​(1)\theta_{\mathrm{CW}}=-72(1) K, resulting in a μeff\mu_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1.97(1) μB\mu_{B} [53]. The large negative θCW\theta_{\mathrm{CW}} confirms dominant AF interactions, and using θCW=2​z​S​(S+1)​𝒥/3\theta_{\rm CW}=2zS(S+1)\mathcal{J}/3 with z=6z=6 the nearest-neighbor coordination number of the pyrochlore lattice, we estimate the exchange coupling constant 𝒥=−24\mathcal{J}=-24 K. The χint\chi_{\rm int} qualitatively follows recent theoretical predictions, although the observed broad maximum at T≈0.12​𝒥T\approx 0.12\mathcal{J} is notably lower in temperature than that predicted by numerical linked cluster expansion (NLCE) results for the disorder free system, at T=0.54​𝒥T=0.54\mathcal{J} [74]. The moment size of μeff=1.97​(1)\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}=1.97(1) μB\mu_{B} is consistent with other Cu2+ systems [45, 35, 55], and close to the theoretical spin-only moment μefftheo=g​J⁡(J+1)​μB\mu^{\rm theo}_{\mathrm{eff}}=g\sqrt{J(J+1)}\mu_{B} = 1.73 μB\mu_{B}, for J=S=12J=S=\frac{1}{2} and g=2g=2 with quenched orbital momentum.

Isothermal magnetization M⁡(H)M(H), seen in Figure 2c, shows a linear AF response at 20 K, and begins to show a Brillouin-like curvature for T≤10T\leq 10 K at fields below 5 T, superimposed on a linear response visible above 5 T. The M⁡(H)M(H) data are well fitted by a superposition of a modified S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Brillouin function corresponding to weakly interacting orphan spins Morp=norp​BJ=1/2​(x′)M_{\rm orp}=n_{\rm orp}B_{J=1/2}(x^{\prime}), and an intrinsic power-law term Mint=A​(μ0​H)αM_{\rm int}=A(\mu_{0}H)^{\alpha} [49, 68, 16]:

M⁡(H)=norp​g​μB2​tanh​(g​μB​μ0​H2​kB​(T−T∗))+A​(μ0​H)αM(H)=\frac{n_{\mathrm{orp}}g\mu_{B}}{2}\mathrm{tanh}\left(\frac{g\mu_{B}\mu_{0}H}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}(T-T^{*})}\right)+A(\mu_{0}H)^{\alpha} (1)

where norpn_{\mathrm{orp}} is the orphan spins fraction, gg is the orphan-spin gg-factor fixed to g=2g=2, T∗T^{*} is the interaction temperature between the orphan spins and α\alpha is the power-law exponent. From the M⁡(H)M(H) fit at 1.8 K, seen in Figure 2d, we extract norpn_{\rm orp} = 0.154(2), T∗T^{*} = 0.30(2) K and α\alpha = 0.73(1), corresponding to ∼\sim15% of weakly ferromagnetically-coupled orphan spins. This norpn_{\rm orp} value was used in the χint=χ−χorp\chi_{\rm int}=\chi-\chi_{\rm orp} subtraction in Figure 2a. From the 1.8 K M⁡(H)M(H) decomposition into MorpM_{\rm orp} and MintM_{\rm int} shown in Figure 2d, we observe a full saturation of the orphan-spin component by μ0​H∼5\mu_{0}H\sim 5 T. The sublinear behaviour α<1\alpha<1 of the intrinsic AF response comes about as a result of the disorder-induced distribution of exchange energies. With this orphan spin fraction norpn_{\rm orp} and the interaction temperature T∗T^{*} fixed to that from the lowest temperature data set where it is best defined, we performed a global fit for M⁡(H)M(H) between 2 and 20 K. The fits are shown as solid lines in Figure 2c. The power-law exponent α\alpha varied between 0.68 and 0.99, indicating a crossover from Brillouin-like to purely linear (α∼1\alpha\sim 1) magnetization at high temperature (see Table S2 in SM [1]).

High-field isothermal magnetization M⁡(H)M(H) in pulsed field up to 60 T, seen in Figure 2e at temperatures between 1.35–50 K, exhibits no plateaus or field-induced transitions predicted for an ideal, disorder-free S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnet [61, 21]. Instead, a rapid low-field (μ0​H<\mu_{0}H< 5 T) polarization of weakly coupled orphan spins is observed at the lowest temperatures, followed by a slow linear polarization of dynamically fluctuating strongly coupled singlets up to 60 T. This behaviour highlights the broad distribution of exchange couplings expected from the RS state, and is consistent with previously-studied RS materials [90, 68, 16]. Even at 60 T we reach only ∼0.6\sim\!0.6 μB\mu_{\rm B}/Cu at 1.35 K, remaining far below full saturation expected for a spin-only Cu2+ ion (μStheo\mu_{S}^{\mathrm{theo}} = 2​S​μB2S\mu_{\rm B} = 1 μB\mu_{\rm B}), underscoring the robustness of strongly bound singlets and persistent fluctuations.

No bifurcation of zero-field-cooled, χZFC\chi_{\rm ZFC}, and field-cooled, χFC\chi_{\rm FC}, magnetic susceptibility measurements was observed down to 1.8 K, indicating no history dependence, in accordance with a dynamic state (see Figure S5 in SM [1]). AC susceptibility, measured with an alternating field amplitude HACH_{\mathrm{AC}} = 0.05 Oe at frequencies between 215 and 10 000 Hz, shows an increase with decreasing temperature without reaching a maximum in the real part, χAC′​(ν,T)\chi^{\prime}_{\mathrm{AC}}(\nu,T), while the imaginary part χAC′′​(ν,T)\chi^{\prime\prime}_{\mathrm{AC}}(\nu,T) remains flat without signs of energy-dissipative processes, see Figure 2f. No frequency dependence was seen in either the real or imaginary parts, ruling out any global collective spin freezing into a static spin-glass ground state down to 0.4 K, despite the sizable magnetic bond disorder present in this material. This is in direct contrast to all previously studied bond-disordered NaA′′​M2A^{\prime\prime}M_{2}F7 pyrochlore fluorides (A′′A^{\prime\prime} = Cd, Ca, Sr; MM = Co, Ni, Mn, Fe), which all reported a glassy ground-state, and a frequency-dependent peak in χAC′​(ν,T)\chi^{\prime}_{\mathrm{AC}}(\nu,T) at Tf≈2−4T_{\mathrm{f}}\approx 2-4 K. [28, 41, 42, 43, 69, 29]

III.3 Specific heat

Specific heat, Cp​(T)C_{p}(T), in zero field shows no sharp first or second order transitions down to 150 mK, ruling out the development of long-range order or global structural changes, however a broad hump is observed at around 1 K, seen in Figure 3a and 3b. This feature shifts to higher temperature with applied field, reminiscent of a Schottky anomaly. After subtraction of the phonon contribution by subtracting the specific heat of the non-magnetic analogue NaCdZn2F7 [28, 29] (black solid line in Figure 3a and 3b) from the total CpC_{p}, the magnetic specific heat Cmag=Cp−Clat≈Cp⁡[NaCdCu2​F7]−Cp⁡[NaCdZn2​F7]C_{\mathrm{mag}}=C_{p}-C_{\rm lat}\approx C_{p\rm[NaCdCu_{2}F_{7}]}-C_{p\rm[NaCdZn_{2}F_{7}\rm]}, and its evolution in applied fields is shown in Figure 2c. The magnetic entropy change Δ​Smag\Delta S_{\rm mag}, calculated by integration of Cmag/TC_{\mathrm{mag}}/T and shown in Figure 3d, reaches only ∼35%\sim\!35\% of the expected value of Rln2, by 100 K. The large missing entropy is a signature of non-magnetic singlet formation combined with residual dynamics at low temperature.

Cmag​(T,H)C_{\rm mag}(T,H) was fitted using a combination of a two-level Schottky anomaly CSchC_{\rm Sch} associated with weakly coupled S=12S=\frac{1}{2} orphan spins, and a power-law term Cpower−law=Apower−law​T1−αCm​a​gC_{\rm power-law}=A_{\rm power-law}T^{1-\alpha_{C_{mag}}} corresponding to the RS phase [38, 54, 26]:

CmagT=ASch​R​Δ2T3​exp⁡(ΔT)(1+exp⁡(ΔT))2+Apower−law​T−αCmag\small\frac{C_{\rm mag}}{T}=A_{\rm Sch}\mathrm{R}\frac{\Delta^{2}}{T^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{exp}\left(\frac{\Delta}{T}\right)}{\left(1+\mathrm{exp}\left(\frac{\Delta}{T}\right)\right)^{2}}+A_{\rm power-law}T^{-\alpha_{C_{\rm mag}}} (2)

The fits to Equation 2 are summarized in Figure 3e, with the individual contributions shown in Figure 3f. We find that αCm​a​g\alpha_{C_{mag}} decreases from 0.87(2) in zero field to 0.28(2) at 9 T, and the extracted Schottky gap Δ\Delta in zero field is 1.34(5) K, suggesting a non-zero splitting of the Cu2+ S=12S=\frac{1}{2} energy levels due to the local internal fields. From the Zeeman formula Δ⁡(H)=g​S​μB​μ0​H\Delta(H)=gS\mu_{B}\mu_{0}H we obtain the slope g​S=1.32​(6)gS=1.32(6), giving the orphan-spin gg-factor g=2.6​(1)g=2.6(1) (see Figure S8 in SM [1]). The orphan spins fraction nophn_{\rm oph} can be estimated from the ratio of the Schottky entropy and total magnetic entropy noph=Δ​SSch/Δ​Smagn_{\rm oph}=\Delta S_{\rm Sch}/\Delta S_{\rm mag}, yielding an apparent increase from ∼10%\sim 10\% in zero field to ∼54%\sim 54\% at 9 T (see Table S4 in SM[1]). This increase does not reflect the creation of new orphan spins. Rather, it arises from the field-induced polarization of weakly bound random singlet pairs, which contribute to the low-temperature Schottky-like feature only once the applied field overcomes their singlet binding energy. In zero field these pairs remain largely inactive, so the intrinsic orphan-spin density is field-independent and best represented by the zero-field value.

At temperatures between 200 and 650 mK, the specific heat shows a power-law dependence Cp∼T1−αCpC_{p}\sim T^{1-\alpha_{C_{p}}} with αCp=0.50​(1)\alpha_{C_{p}}=0.50(1), followed by a TT-linear specific heat Cp=γ​TC_{p}=\gamma T below 200 mK, with γ\gamma = 0.64(2) J K-2 mol-Cu-1, see Figure 3g. The crossover to the linear regime at the lowest temperatures is a characteristic thermodynamic signature of the RS state [88, 86, 87, 85, 32, 31]. In close analogy to the Sommerfeld coefficient in metals, the linear specific-heat coefficient γ\gamma in QSL/RS Mott insulators is proportional to the density of low-energy magnetic excitations in the zero-energy limit, consistent with a gapless excitation spectrum. In Figure 3h, we observe a constant Cp/TC_{p}/T below 200 mK in zero field corresponding to the Cp/T=γC_{p}/T=\gamma regime, and an emerging sharp peak in applied 0.1–0.5 T fields, which shifts to higher temperature with increasing field. The emergence of a sharp low-temperature peak in Cp/TC_{p}/T under small applied magnetic fields may indicate the development of short-range correlations involving orphan spins, stabilized by the suppression of low-energy random singlet fluctuations.

III.4 Muon spin relaxation (μ\muSR)

Spin dynamics were characterized down to 58 mK using local-probe μ\muSR experiments. Zero-field measurements revealed oscillations coming from the F-–μ+\mu^{+}–F- bound complex, commonly seen in fluoride materials [7, 8, 92]. The base-temperature ZF muon relaxation can be seen in Figure 4a, and the temperature dependence of ZF-μ\muSR is shown Figure 4b. The ZF spectra were fitted using a simple exponential function multiplied by a modified, phase-shifted ZF F-μ\mu-F function GF−μ−F​(t)G_{\rm F-\mu-F}(t):

AZF​(t)=A0​GF−μ−F​(t)​exp​(−λZF​t)+AbaseA_{\rm ZF}(t)=A_{0}G_{\rm F-\mu-F}(t)\mathrm{exp}(-\lambda_{\rm ZF}t)+A_{\rm base} (3)

where A0A_{0} is the relaxing amplitude, λZF\lambda_{\rm ZF} is the zero-field muon relaxation rate, AbaseA_{\rm base} is a non-relaxing constant baseline and the ZF F-μ\mu-F function GF−μ−FG_{F-\mu-F} has the form [7]

GF−μ−F(t)=16[\displaystyle G_{\rm F-\mu-F}(t)=\frac{1}{6}\Big[\; 3+cos⁡(3​ωd​t+ϕ)\displaystyle 3+\cos(\sqrt{3}\,\omega_{d}t+\phi)
+(1−13)​cos⁡(3−32​ωd​t+ϕ)\displaystyle+\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{3-\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\omega_{d}t+\phi\right)
+(1+13)cos(3+32ωdt+ϕ)].\displaystyle+\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\omega_{d}t+\phi\right)\Big]. (4)

Here, ϕ\phi is the phase shift and ωd\omega_{d} is the dipolar interaction frequency. On cooling from 10 K in zero field, the F-–μ+\mu^{+}–F- oscillations are damped by electronic fluctuations slowing into the time-window of the muon. This exponential damping increases significantly below ∼3\sim\!3 K, indicating a rapid slowing of the spin fluctuation rate, but plateaus below ∼0.7\sim\!0.7 K - a hallmark of continued quantum fluctuations [94, 50], see Figure 4d. This plateau is also seen in measurements in an applied 200 G longitudinal field, used to decouple the muons from the static dipolar fields of the F-–μ+\mu^{+}–F- state, seen in Figure 4d. However, the cleaner spectra, shown in Figure 4c, highlight a decay of asymmetry at low temperatures that is not purely exponential, but instead show a Gaussian shoulder at t<3t<3 μ\mus, and are better fitted by a stretched exponential function

ALF​(t)=A0​exp​(−(λLF​t)βLF)+Abase,A_{\rm LF}(t)=A_{0}\mathrm{exp}(-(\lambda_{\rm LF}t)^{\beta_{\rm LF}})+A_{\rm base}, (5)

where A0A_{0} is the relaxing amplitude, λLF\lambda_{\rm LF} is the LF muon relaxation rate, βLF\beta_{\rm LF} is the stretching exponent and AbaseA_{\rm base} is a non-relaxing constant baseline. The stretched-exponential relaxation indicates an inhomogeneous mixture of both dynamic and partially frozen local fields. This can be explained by a slowing of dynamics of the weakly interacting orphan spins below 1 K within the RS matrix [89, 15, 68]. The inhomogeneous distribution of local fields is tracked using the stretching exponent, βLF\beta_{\rm LF}, in Figure 4d. At higher-longitudinal fields these weakly interacting frozen orphan spins are fully polarized and the spectra return to a purely exponential relaxation, shown in Figure 4a, confirming continued spin-dynamics even at 58 mK.

III.5 Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)

To complement the μ\muSR results, 23Na NMR measurements were performed between 120 mK and 150 K in fields of 0.67 T and 3 T. 23Na occupies the axially symmetric AA site (point group 3¯​m\bar{3}m), where it is statistically distributed with Cd2+ with equal probability. As shown in Figure 5a and 5b, the spectra exhibit a single broad peak with broad tails on both sides. The spectral shape likely reflects a broadened I=32I\!=\!\frac{3}{2} powder pattern, in which the Na/Cd site distribution merges the central and quadrupolar satellite transitions. In the related compound NaCaCo2F7, the 23Na nuclear quadrupole frequency was reported to be of the order of νQ\nu_{Q}(23Na) ∼\sim 1 MHz [71]. At every temperature, the nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate 1/T11/T_{1} was measured at the position of the resonance peak by fitting the recovery curves with a stretched exponential function:

M⁡(∞)−M⁡(t)M⁡(∞)=0.4​exp⁡{−(t/T1)βNMR}\displaystyle\frac{M(\infty)-M(t)}{M(\infty)}=0.4\exp\{-\left(t/T_{1}\right)^{\beta_{\rm NMR}}\}
+0.6​exp⁡{−(6​t/T1)βNMR},\displaystyle+0.6\exp\{-\left(6t/T_{1}\right)^{\beta_{\rm NMR}}\}, (6)

assuming that only the central transition was saturated while the populations of satellite transitions remain unaffected. The temperature dependence of the extracted 1/T11/T_{1} and βNMR\beta_{\rm NMR} values is summarized in Figure 5c and 5d.

The stretching exponent βNMR\beta_{\rm NMR} relates to the spatial distribution of T1T_{1}, with βNMR≈1\beta_{\rm NMR}\!\approx\!1 above 100 K implying uniform relaxation, and a decreasing βNMR<1\beta_{\rm NMR}<1 below 100 K signaling inhomogeneous dynamics. At 0.67 T, both βNMR\beta_{\rm NMR} and 1/T11/T_{1} exhibit a broad ∼\sim1 K hump (seen in Figure 5c and 5d), consistent with the broad anomaly in CpC_{p} and the increases of λμ​SR\lambda_{\mu{\rm SR}} and βμ​SR\beta_{\mu{\rm SR}} near 1 K. Moreover, for 0.67 T the spectral intensity multiplied by temperature I×TI\times T drops below ∼\sim1 K without a shape change (seen in Figure 5a), pointing to an inhomogeneous distribution of static internal fields as also seen by μ\muSR. The intensity loss likely reflects a subset of 23Na sites experiencing static fields that broaden or shift the resonance, leaving the low-TT signal from 23Na near Cu moments that remain dynamic. In contrast, at 3 T the I×TI\times T is nearly temperature-independent because the orphan spins that were responsible for the static-field broadening at 0.67 T are now mostly polarized, as can be inferred from the orphan-spin Brillouin function in Figure 2d. Correspondingly, the ∼\sim1 K anomaly in βNMR\beta_{\rm NMR} is suppressed at 3 T, and the 1/T11/T_{1} hump is smoothed and shifts to higher temperature.

III.6 Scaling behaviour

We now turn to the scaling behaviour and data collapse of measured physical quantities χ⁡(T)\chi(T), Cmag/TC_{\rm mag}/T and (1/T1T)23{}^{23}(1/T_{1}T) in T/(μ0​H)T/(\mu_{0}H), as well as M⁡(H)M(H) in (μ0​H)/T(\mu_{0}H)/T and P⁡(t)P(t) in t/(μ0​H)ημ​SRt/(\mu_{0}H)^{\eta_{\rm\mu SR}}. This behaviour provides the smoking gun evidence for the RS ground state in NaCdCu2F7, in agreement with the scaling theory for S=12S=\frac{1}{2} frustrated quantum magnets with quenched disorder [37, 38, 14].

In Figure 6a, we show the temperature-dependent DC susceptibility in multiple fields, on a log-log scale. χ⁡(T)\chi(T) exhibits two distinct power-law regimes as χ⁡(T)∼T−αχ\chi(T)\sim T^{-\alpha_{\chi}}: a field-independent regime above 10 K with αχ=0.75​(1)\alpha_{\chi}=0.75(1), as well as a field-dependent regime below 10 K with varying αχ\alpha_{\chi} = 0.15(1) – 0.68(1), decreasing with applied field as χ⁡(T)\chi(T) flattens upon polarization of the orphan spins. In addition, the susceptibility data in different fields collapse onto a single curve after scaling by field (μ0​H)αχ​χ​(T)(\mu_{0}H)^{\alpha_{\chi}}\chi(T) as a function of T/(μ0​H)T/(\mu_{0}H), with αχ=0.74\alpha_{\chi}=0.74, see Figure 6b. Figure 6c shows the data collapse of isothermal magnetization at temperatures between 1.8 and 20 K, onto a single curve after scaling by temperature M​TαM−1MT^{\alpha_{M}-1} as a function of μ0​H/T\mu_{0}H/T [38]. This displays a perfect data collapse for αM=0.73\alpha_{M}=0.73, in agreement with the fitted exponent in the power-law term in Equation 1. Furthermore, in Figure 6d, we observe a data collapse of magnetic specific heat scaled by field (μ0​H)αC​Cmag/T(\mu_{0}H)^{\alpha_{C}}C_{\rm mag}/T as a function of T/(μ0​H)T/(\mu_{0}H) for αC=0.68\alpha_{C}=0.68. Strikingly, the power-law scaling also applies to the muon relaxation rate λLF∼(μ0​HL​F)−ημ​SR\lambda_{\rm LF}\sim(\mu_{0}H_{LF})^{-\eta_{\rm\mu SR}} acquired from fitting the field-dependent spectra between 200 and 3000 G by a stretched exponential function (see Figure S9 and S10 in SM [1]). Here, ημ​SR=1−αμ​SR\eta_{\rm\mu SR}=1-\alpha_{\rm\mu SR} = 0.26(2), giving αμ​SR=0.74​(2)\alpha_{\rm\mu SR}=0.74(2). This leads to a data collapse of the field-dependent muon polarization spectra P⁡(t)=(ALF​(t)−Abase)/A0P(t)=(A_{\rm LF}(t)-A_{\rm base})/A_{0} when plotted as a function of t/(μ0​H)ημ​SRt/(\mu_{0}H)^{\eta_{\rm\mu SR}}, see Figure 6e. The observed power-law behaviour is a result of a power-law decaying spin-spin correlation function S⁡(t)∼t−(1−α)S(t)\sim t^{-(1-\alpha)} governed by a power-law spectral density S⁡(ω)∼ω−αS(\omega)\sim\omega^{-\alpha} [65], which have been reported in several other QSL candidates with spin chain, pyrochlore, kagome, and triangular lattices [65, 48, 33, 34, 50]. The power-law scaling is also evident in the 23Na NMR as 1/T1∼TηNMR1/T_{1}\sim T^{\eta_{\rm NMR}}, exhibiting ηNMR\eta_{\rm NMR} = 1.34(7) at 0.67 T below 400 mK, and ηNMR\eta_{\rm NMR} = 2.41(4) at 3 T below 1 K (see Figure 5c), consistent with other RS and QSL candidates [47, 78]. This leads to a data collapse of (1/T1T)23{}^{23}(1/T_{1}T) scaled by field (μ0​H)αNMR​(1/T1​T)(\mu_{0}H)^{\alpha_{\rm NMR}}(1/T_{1}T) as a function of T/(μ0​H)T/(\mu_{0}H) for αNMR=1.35\alpha_{\rm NMR}=1.35, see Figure 6f. We note that the exponent αNMR=1.35\alpha_{\rm NMR}=1.35 is approximately double in value compared to αχ\alpha_{\chi}, αM\alpha_{M}, αC\alpha_{C} or αμ​SR\alpha_{\mu\rm SR}. While the bulk probes χ⁡(T)\chi(T), M⁡(H)M(H) or Cmag/TC_{\rm mag}/T reflect the static density of low-energy excitations, the quantity (1/T1​T)∼∑q|Aq|2​(χ′′​(q,ω0)/ω0)ω0→0(1/T_{1}T)\sim\sum\limits_{\textbf{q}}|A_{\textbf{q}}|^{2}\left(\chi^{\prime\prime}(\textbf{q},\omega_{0})/\omega_{0}\right)_{\omega_{0}\rightarrow 0} is proportional to the momentum q-averaged imaginary part of the local spin susceptibility, reflecting the low-frequency spectral weight of spin fluctuations. Although LF-μ\muSR also probes the low-frequency limit of the dynamical susceptibility as λLF∼∑q|Aqμ|2​(χ′′​(q,ωμ)/ωμ)ωμ→0\lambda_{\rm LF}\sim\sum\limits_{\textbf{q}}|A^{\mu}_{\textbf{q}}|^{2}\left(\chi^{\prime\prime}(\textbf{q},\omega_{\mu})/\omega_{\mu}\right)_{\omega_{\mu}\rightarrow 0}, the αμ​SR=0.74​(2)\alpha_{\mu\rm SR}=0.74(2) exponent agrees more with the bulk-probe exponents rather than αNMR\alpha_{\rm NMR}. We attribute this to the different frequency windows in which these probes operate: LF-μ\muSR is sensitive to fluctuations in the ∼105\sim 10^{5}–10710^{7} Hz range set by the muon gyromagnetic ratio (ωμ=γμ​HLF\omega_{\mu}=\gamma_{\mu}H_{\rm LF}), whereas 23Na NMR probes dynamics at the Larmor frequency at ∼107\sim 10^{7}–10810^{8} Hz (ω0=γNa23​HLF\omega_{0}={}^{23}\!\gamma_{\mathrm{Na}}H_{\rm LF}). In a random singlet system with a broad distribution of excitation energies, the ultra-low-frequency window accessed by LF-μ\muSR emphasizes the same low-energy excitations that dominate bulk thermodynamics, while NMR probes higher-frequency dynamics, resulting in different scaling exponents.

III.7 Conclusion

In summary, using a plethora of complementary bulk and local-probe techniques, we have shown that the frustrated, magnetic-bond-disordered S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCu2F7 does not exhibit long-range magnetic order or global spin freezing down to 58 mK. Instead, the observed power-law scaling behaviour and data collapse across multiple experimental probes are consistent with a random singlet ground state characterized by a broad distribution of exchange couplings, noted by the coexistence of singlet dimers and weakly coupled orphan spins. This behavior originates from intrinsic Na+/Cd2+ disorder on the pyrochlore AA site, which modifies the Cu2+-F--Cu2+ superexchange pathways on the magnetic, pyrochlore BB-site sublattice. The absence of spin-glass freezing contrasts with previously studied NaA′′​B2A^{\prime\prime}B_{2}F7 pyrochlore fluorides [28, 29, 41, 42, 43, 69], where comparable magnetic bond disorder leads to glassy ground states, suggesting that strong S=12S=\tfrac{1}{2} quantum fluctuations play an important role in suppressing spin freezing in NaCdCu2F7 and stabilizing a quantum-disordered state.

The present study establishes NaCdCu2F7 as a well-characterized example of disorder-driven quantum magnetism, but several important questions remain. All measurements reported here were performed on polycrystalline samples, and the growth of high-quality single crystals would enable momentum-resolved and anisotropic measurements. Thermal transport experiments would be particularly valuable for probing low-energy excitations and further distinguishing random singlet behavior from other quantum-disordered states. Neutron scattering studies would provide direct access to the dynamic spin structure factor; however, such experiments are presently hindered by the strong neutron absorption of Cd, motivating isotopic enrichment or the investigation of chemically related pyrochlore fluorides such as NaCaCu2F7 or NaSrCu2F7.

Finally, recent theoretical work has shown that entanglement-sensitive quantities such as quantum Fisher information (QFI), extracted from experimentally accessible correlation functions [79], may distinguish random singlet states from quantum spin liquids even when thermodynamic signatures are similar. Applying such approaches to NaCdCu2F7 and related materials represents an interesting direction for future experimental and theoretical studies.

Supplementary materials: Random singlet physics in the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCu2F7

I Sample preparation & crystal growth attempt

Polycrystalline NaCdCu2F7 was prepared by mixing and grinding a stoichiometric mix of dry, high-purity precursor binary fluorides (Thermofisher Scientific 99.99% NaF metals basis, 99.5% CuF2 anhydrous and 99.99% CdF2 metals basis). This was done inside a glovebox with an argon atmosphere to prevent absorption of air moisture that would lead to possible oxidation at elevated temperatures. The mixture was filled into a hollow tubular graphite crucible and mounted inside an optical floating zone furnace (Crystal Systems Corp. FZ-T-4000-VI-VPM-PC). An initial pre-reaction was done by rapidly melting at ∼\sim 700 inside a dynamic (0.25 l/min) high-pressure (8 bar) argon atmosphere, heating the graphite at 100 mm/hr in the up-down-up direction along the whole crucible length. This was repeated several times with intermittent grindings. The graphite crucible served as a vessel suitable for accommodating highly reactive melted fluorides, as well as a purifying agent to react with possible oxide impurities present in the precursor chemicals. Lastly, single-crystal growth was attempted by grinding the pre-melted polycrystalline rod and filling it into a fresh graphite crucible, then slow melting at 2 mm/hr at ∼\sim 700 in the same dynamic argon atmosphere. However, no large single crystals could be obtained. Instead, a high-purity polycrystalline NaCdCu2F7 rod was formed and ground into a fine powder for further measurements. Upon crushing the polycrystalline rod, small crystallites were isolated and used for structure solution using single crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD). To confirm that the crystal structure solved by SCXRD is representative of the bulk, a section of the recrystallized rod was crushed and checked by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD).

II Powder and single crystal X-ray diffraction

A small crystallite, selected from the crushed recrystallized rod, was mounted on a glass fiber and measured at 300 K using a Rigaku Xcalibur Gemini ultra-diffractometer, with graphite-monochromated Mo Kα\alpha (λ\lambda = 0.71073 Å) radiation, and an Atlas S2 CCD detector. Diffraction data were integrated using CrysAlis Pro [60] with an analytical numeric absorption correction combined with a multifaceted crystal model and an empirical absorption correction using spherical harmonics. The structure was solved by charge flipping using Superflip [63] and refined by full-matrix least squares in Jana2020 [64]. Structural graphics were created using Jana2020 and Vesta [52]. Supplementary crystallographic data can be obtained free of charge in the CIF deposited in the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre (https://www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/structures/), deposit number 2487621.

The crystal structure of Na(1+x)Cd(1-x)Cu2F(7-x) is of the pyrochlore A2​B2​X6​X′A_{2}B_{2}X_{6}X^{\prime} type and has only been reported once in a successful synthesis and powder X-ray diffraction report [22]. Similar reported structures are stoichiometric and fully fluorinated, with ions A=A′⁣+0.5A′′2+0.5A=A^{\prime+}_{0.5}A^{\prime\prime 2+}_{0.5} (A′⁣+A^{\prime+} = Na, A′′2+A^{\prime\prime 2+} = Ca, Sr, Cd) sharing position with half occupancy each, and they crystallize in a cubic unit cell, space group F​d​3¯​mFd\overline{3}m. The SCXRD measurement and refinement details of Na1.076Cd0.924Cu2F6.924 are summarized in Table S1, and the structure is shown in Figure S1. It crystallizes in a cubic unit cell with aa = 10.3038(15) Å, space group F​d​3¯​mFd\overline{3}m. Inspection of the reciprocal space map cuts along the (h​k​0),(h​0​l)(hk0),(h0l) and (0​k​l)(0kl) planes reveals no superstructure reflections, which would indicate occupational ordering of Na+ and Cd2+ on the pyrochlore AA site (see Figure S2). An initial refinement of Na(1+x)Cd(1-x)Cu2F(7-x) with Na and Cd occupancies fixed at 0.5 each gave residue values RR(obs) = 2.63%\% and GOF(obs) = 3.12. Refinement of the Cd occupancy decreased the residue values to RR(obs) = 2.19%\% and GOF(obs) = 1.91, which led to the conclusion that the AA site is Cd deficient. Chemical balance can be achieved either by having Cu3+ sharing the BB site with Cu2+ [25] or F1 deficiency [24].

According to the magnetic properties of NaCdCu2F7 (the experimental effective moment μeffexp\mu^{\rm exp}_{\rm eff} = 1.97 μB\mu_{B} being close to the theoretical Cu2+ spin-only value 1.73 μB\mu_{B}) and given that Cu3+ is unlikely to be present in the sample, the occupancy of F1 was refined and resulted in RR(obs) = 2.10%\% and GOF(obs) = 1.89. Na occupancy was restricted so that site AA has full occupancy when summing Na and Cd, while F1 was refined as a function of the Cd occupancy. Refinement of the occupancies changed neither the bond lengths, which were within 3σ\sigma (see Figure S3 and Table S2), nor the CuF6 and Na/CdF8 polyhedra. The BB site octahedron (CuF6) is slightly deformed and has six equal bond lengths, which causes the F-Cu-F bond angle to deviate from the ideal 90∘ to 97.22(8)∘.

A small section of the recrystallized rod obtained by the optical floating zone growth, representative of the bulk, was crushed into a fine powder and analyzed by powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) using a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometer with CuKα1\alpha_{1} and CuKα2\alpha_{2} radiation (λ=1.5418\lambda=1.5418 Å), and a structural Rietveld refinement was performed using Topas Academic V6 [12]. The PXRD pattern of NaCdCu2F7 is shown in Figure S4.

III DC Magnetization

DC magnetization measurements on powdered NaCdCu2F7 were performed in a Quantum Design Magnetic Property Measurement System (model MPMS-XL 7 T), using the reciprocating sample option (RSO).

In the left panel of Figure S5, we show the DC magnetic susceptibility χ⁡(T)=M⁡(T)/H\chi(T)=M(T)/H measured in μ0​H=\mu_{0}H= 0.67 T, 3 T and 7 T fields between 1.8 and 300 K. As discussed in the main text, we observe a diverging Curie-like tail at low temperature coming about from the paramagnetic orphan spins in the material. With applied field, the low-temperature tail gets supressed and begins to show curvature as we saturate the orphan spins contribution. No magnetic transition or spin freezing is observed in χ⁡(T)\chi(T) down to 1.8 K. This is proven by measuring the zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and field-cooled (FC) susceptibility in a small applied field of 100 Oe (0.01 T) – we see no bifurcation of χZFC​(T)\chi_{\rm ZFC}(T) and χFC​(T)\chi_{\rm FC}(T), indicating a dynamic state without any history dependence (right panel of Figure S5).

Isothermal magnetization M⁡(H)M(H) was measured between 1.8 and 20 K in fields up to 7 T. No hysteresis effects were observed, instead we observe a superposition of a Brillouin contribution from weakly interacting orphan spins and an intrinsic antiferromagnetic response from the random singlet phase. As discussed in the main text, the data were fitted using a modified S=12S=\frac{1}{2} Brillouin function and a power-law term:

M⁡(H)=norp​g​μB2​tanh​(g​μB​μ0​H2​kB​(T−T∗))+A​(μ0​H)αM(H)=\frac{n_{\mathrm{orp}}g\mu_{B}}{2}\mathrm{tanh}\left(\frac{g\mu_{B}\mu_{0}H}{2k_{\mathrm{B}}(T-T^{*})}\right)+A(\mu_{0}H)^{\alpha} (1)

Initially, a fit was performed on the 1.8 K data, yielding a norpn_{\rm orp} = 15.4(2) % fraction of weakly ferromagnetically coupled (T∗T^{*} = 0.30(2) K) orphan spins, and an exponent αM\alpha_{M} = 0.728(15) for the intinsic power-law response. The orphan spins fraction norpn_{\rm orp} and the interaction temperature T∗T^{*} were then fixed and a global fit was performed on M⁡(H)M(H) for temperatures between 2 and 20 K. The fits are shown in the main text in Figure 2c , with a decomposition of the 1.8 K fit into the Brillouin and intrinsic component in Figure 2d. The fitted parameters are summarized in Table S3.

The orphan spins contribution χorp\chi_{\rm orp} was then subtracted from the magnetic susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) at 0.67 T, 3 T and 7 T, resulting in the intrinsic susceptibility χint=χ−χorp\chi_{\rm int}=\chi-\chi_{\rm orp} (see Figure S6). At 0.67 T we notice a broad maximum in χint\chi_{\rm int} around 3 K, which gets suppressed and shifts to higher temperature with applied field. In the bottom panel of Figure S6 we plot the inverse susceptibility χ−1​(T)\chi^{-1}(T) and χint−1​(T)\chi_{\rm int}^{-1}(T). Performing the Curie-Weiss fit on the inverse intrinsic susceptibility χint−1=(χ−χorp)−1\chi_{\rm int}^{-1}=(\chi-\chi_{\rm orp})^{-1} at 0.67 T between 200 and 300 K, we extract CC = 0.427(1) emu K mol-1 Oe-1, θCW=−93​(1)\theta_{\mathrm{CW}}=-93(1) K and μeff\mu_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1.85(1) μB\mu_{B}, corresponding to g=2.14​(1)g=2.14(1).

High-field isothermal magnetization was measured in the High Magnetic Field Laboratory (Hochfeld-Magnetlabor Dresden, HLD) in the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) in Dresden, Germany. A pulsed 60 T magnet was utilized, with a cryostat setup allowing us to measure MM(HH) between 1.35 and 50 K. The powdered NaCdCu2F7 was stuffed inside a kapton tube, which was attached to a sample holder and inserted into the magnetometer inside the cryostat. The magnetometer consists of two pick-up coils, balanced carefully to subtract the magnet-pulse background from the sample signal. The high-field magnetization data measured on sweeping up the field are shown in the main text in Figure 2e.

IV AC susceptibility

Temperature and frequency dependent AC susceptibility was measured between 0.4 and 4 K using a custom-made coil for the 3He option in a Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS). An oscillating field with a HACH_{\rm AC} = 0.05 Oe amplitude was used, with no additional external applied field. The used frequency range was 10 – 10 000 Oe, equidistant on a logarithmic scale. To acquire reasonable statistics, frequencies between 10 and 464.2 Hz were measured with 5000 repetitions, and frequencies between 1000 and 10 000 Hz were measured using a 5 second counting time. The data are summarized in the main text in Figure 2f. Frequencies below 100 Hz have been ommitted due to a large noise contribution.

V Heat capacity

Heat capacity was measured between 1.8 K and 300 K via the heat relaxation method in the PPMS, with the addition of a 3He low-temperature insert for temperatures between 0.4 and 20 K. A Quantum Design heat capacity puck with a non-magnetic sapphire stage was utilized, using a small amount of Apiezon-N grease for attaching the polished piece of polycrystalline NaCdCu2F7 to the platform. The apiezon contribution to specific heat was subsequently removed. An Oxford Instruments Triton dilution refrigerator was employed for zero-field and in-field sub-1 K heat capacity measurements. For the estimation of the magnetic component of specific heat, the subtraction of the phonon contribution from the lattice was performed using a non-magnetic analogue NaCdZn2F7 (similarly as for NaCdCo2F7, NaCdNi2F7 and NaCdMn2F7 [28, 29]), with some scaling necessary to accommodate for the differing unit cell volume:

Cmag=Cp−Clat≈Cp⁡[NaCdCu2​F7]−Cp⁡[NaCdZn2​F7]C_{\rm mag}=C_{p}-C_{\rm lat}\approx C_{p\rm[NaCdCu_{2}F_{7}]}-C_{p\rm[NaCdZn_{2}F_{7}]} (2)

In the left panel of Figure S7, we see the zero field specific heat CpC_{p} of NaCdCu2F7 between 1.8 and 100 K, with the scaled CpC_{p} of the non-magnetic analogue NaCdZn2F7 (black solid line) for eventual subtraction of phonon contribution. In the inset, we zoom in to the 3He specific heat measured between 0.4 and 20 K in fields up to 9 T. We see a broad anomaly centered around 1 K, which shifts to higher temperature with applied field. In the right panel of Figure S7, we show the specific heat divided by temperature Cp/TC_{p}/T in different fields. We observe an emerging peak in Cp/TC_{p}/T below 1 K, which flattens and shifts to higher temperature with applied field. Both the zero-field and in-field data overlap above 15 K, suggesting a dominant phonon contribution above this temperature.

The extracted magnetic specific heat CmagC_{\rm mag} and Cmag/TC_{\rm mag}/T are shown in the main text in Figure 3c and 3d. We observe a broad peak shifting to higher temperature with applied field, which comes from a combination of a Schottky anomaly of the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} orphan spins and an intrinsic random-singlet term. We can fit the data using a two-level Schottky anomaly and a power-law term corresponding to the random singlet phase [38, 26]:

Cmag=CSch+Cpower−lawC_{\rm mag}=C_{\rm Sch}+C_{\rm power-law} (3)

Taking the standard formula for a two-level Schottky system and Cpower−law=Apower−law​T1−αCmagC_{\rm power-law}=A_{\rm power-law}T^{1-\alpha_{C_{\rm mag}}}, we then fit the Cmag/TC_{\rm mag}/T data as follows:

CmagT=ASch​R​Δ2T3​exp⁡(ΔT)(1+exp⁡(ΔT))2+Apower−law​T−αCmag\frac{C_{\rm mag}}{T}=A_{\rm Sch}\mathrm{R}\frac{\Delta^{2}}{T^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{exp}\left(\frac{\Delta}{T}\right)}{\left(1+\mathrm{exp}\left(\frac{\Delta}{T}\right)\right)^{2}}+A_{\rm power-law}T^{-\alpha_{C_{\rm mag}}} (4)

where Δ\Delta is the energy gap and αCmag\alpha_{C_{\rm mag}} is the power-law exponent. The fits are shown in Figure S8, with the fitted parameters summarized in Table S4. In the left inset of Figure S8, we see the field dependence of the Schottky gap Δ⁡(H)\Delta(H) as well as the scaling parameter ASchA_{\rm Sch}. We fit the field dependence of the Schottky gap with the Zeeman splitting formula Δ⁡(H)=g​S​μB​μ0​H\Delta(H)=gS\mu_{B}\mu_{0}H and extract the slope g​SgS = 1.32(6), corresponding to the gg-factor for the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} orphan spins gg = 2.6(1). In the right panel of Figure S8, we see the field dependence of the exponent αpower−law\alpha_{\rm power-law} and the scaling factor Apower−lawA_{\rm power-law}. Both parameters decrease with applied field, the power-law exponent changing from 0.87(2) in zero field to 0.28(2) at 9 T.

By integrating the Schottky contribution Δ​SSch=∫0.420CSchT​𝑑T\Delta S_{\rm Sch}=\int_{0.4}^{20}\frac{C_{\rm Sch}}{T}dT and the magnetic specific heat Δ​Smag=∫0.420CmagT​𝑑T\Delta S_{\rm mag}=\int_{0.4}^{20}\frac{C_{\rm mag}}{T}dT between 0.4 and 20 K, we get the respective magnetic entropy changes. We can estimate the fraction of orphan spins by taking the ratio norp=Δ​SSchΔ​Smagn_{\rm orp}=\frac{\Delta S_{\rm Sch}}{\Delta S_{\rm mag}}. In Table S4, we see that the orphan spins fraction norpn_{\rm orp} changes from ∼10%\sim 10\% in zero field to ∼54%\sim 54\penalty\ \% in 9 T field.

VI Muon spin relaxation (μ\muSR)

Muon spin relaxation spectroscopy measurements were performed at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory in Harwell Oxford, United Kingdom. The MuSR instrument was used, utilising a dilution refrigerator (50 mK - 4 K) cryostat setup. Approximately 600 mg of powdered phase-pure NaCdCu2F7 was spread onto a silver plate, with a small addition of a dilute GE varnish to stick the thin layer of powder to the surface, and enclosed with a second Ag plate from the top. The sample-containing Ag block was then attached to the sample stick and inserted into the dilution refrigerator cryostat in the MuSR instrument. A TF20 (20 Gauss transverse field) measurement was performed at 10 K to calibrate the asymmetry parameter between the front and back detectors. The sample was then cooled down to the base temperature (50 mK), where the isothermal field dependence (0 - 3000 G) of the muon asymmetry spectra was taken. Afterwards, the temperature dependence (50 mK - 4 K) of both zero-field and longitudinal-field muon asymmetry spectra were collected, see Figure 4 in the main text. The spectra were fitted using the WiMDA and Mantid software. [66, 3]

The base-temperature (50 mK) isothermal field dependence of μ\muSR spectra can be seen in Figure S9. In the left panel, we see the 0–200 G field dependence. We notice oscillations coming from the F-μ\mu-F complex, as expected in all fluoride materials [7]. The static fields coming from the F-μ\mu-F dipole-dipole interaction can be decoupled by applying a small longitudinal field (LF), as we suppress the oscillations to a shorter time window with increasing field, eventually fully decoupling this effect with the application of LF 200 G. In the right panel of Figure S9, we see the isothermal field dependence at 50 mK between 200 and 3000 G after fully decoupling the F-μ\mu-F oscillations. We observe a Gaussian shoulder below t<t< 3 μ\mus for fields between 200 and 1000 G, suggesting the presence of some static internal fields likely from a frozen subset of orphan spins or dimer singlets. As we increase the field to 1500 G and above, we fully decouple the static internal fields and observe a fully exponential relaxation of asymmetry, suggesting a fully dynamic state. We fit the spectra using a stretched exponential function A⁡(t)=A0​exp​(−(λLF​t)β)+AbaseA(t)=A_{0}\mathrm{exp}(-(\lambda_{\rm LF}t)^{\beta})+A_{\rm base}, where A0A_{0} is the relaxing amplitude, λLF\lambda_{\rm LF} is the muon relaxation rate, β\beta is the stretching exponent and AbaseA_{\rm base} is the non-relaxing constant baseline. In Figure S10, we plot the muon relaxation rate λLF\lambda_{\rm LF} as a function of the applied field μ0​HLF\mu_{0}H_{\rm LF} on a log-log scale (left panel), as well as the inverse 1/λLF1/\lambda_{\rm LF} as a function of HLF2H^{2}_{\rm LF} on a linear scale. We observe a power-law decay of muon relaxation rate λLF∼(μ0​HLF)αμ​SR−1\lambda_{\rm LF}\sim(\mu_{0}H_{\rm LF})^{{\alpha_{\mu\rm SR}}-1} with αμ​SR\alpha_{\mu\rm SR} = 0.74(2). This leads to a data collapse of the field-dependent muon spectra when plotted as polarization P⁡(t)=(A⁡(t)−Abase)/A0P(t)=(A(t)-A_{\rm base})/A_{0} as a function of time scaled by field, t/(μ0​H)ημ​SRt/(\mu_{0}H)^{\eta_{\mu\rm SR}}, for ημ​SR=1−αμ​SR=0.26​(2)\eta_{\mu\rm SR}=1-\alpha_{\mu\rm SR}=0.26(2), see Figure 6e in the main text.

Furthermore, the (μ0​HLF)2(\mu_{0}H_{\rm LF})^{2} dependence of 1/λLF1/\lambda_{\rm LF} (right panel of Figure S10) can be seen for fields between 1000 and 3000 G. The high-field regime can be analyzed using the Bloembergen Purcell and Pound (BPP) theory, which assumes simple spin dynamics with an exponentially decaying spin-spin autocorrelation function ⟨S⁡(t)​S​(0)⟩∼e−ν​t\langle S(t)S(0)\rangle\sim e^{-\nu t}, for which:

λLF=2​γμ2​Hfluc2​νν2+γμ2​HLF2\lambda_{\rm LF}=\frac{2\gamma_{\mu}^{2}H^{2}_{\mathrm{fluc}}\nu}{\nu^{2}+\gamma_{\mu}^{2}H_{\mathrm{LF}}^{2}} (5)

where γμ\gamma_{\mu} = 135.538 MHz/T is the muon gyromagnetic ratio, HflucH_{\mathrm{fluc}} is the internal fluctuating field and ν\nu is the fluctuating frequency. From our BPP fit for fields between 1500 and 3000 G, we get HflucH_{\mathrm{fluc}} = 191(7) G and ν\nu = 61(5) MHz.

VII Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)

NMR measurements in the temperature range of 1.8 - 150 K were performed using a 4He variable-temperature insert (VTI) installed in a superconducting magnet dedicated to NMR, together with a phase-coherent, pulsed spectrometer. For measurements between 120 mK and 2.1 K, a 3He-4He dilution-refrigerator probe head was operated in the VTI. The excitation coil was custom-wound from silver wire. Frequency-swept spectra at different constant fields were obtained with the radio frequency (r.f.) circuit tuned and matched at each point. Nuclear spin echoes were generated using a standard 90°\degree - 180°\degree pulse sequence, with a first-pulse duration of 2-3 μ\mus for the 4He cryostat range and 10-20 μ\mus for the dilution cryostat range; the r.f. power was optimized for each spectral peak. The interpulse delay τ\tau was typically 20-30 μ\mus. Each echo signal was accumulated and Fourier transformed to obtain the spectra.

For every temperature, the nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate 1/T11/T_{1} was measured at the position of the resonance peak by fitting the recovery curves with a stretched exponential function:

M⁡(∞)−M⁡(t)M⁡(∞)=0.4​exp⁡{−(t/T1)βNMR}+0.6​exp⁡{−(6​t/T1)βNMR},\frac{M(\infty)-M(t)}{M(\infty)}=0.4\exp\{-\left(t/T_{1}\right)^{\beta_{\rm NMR}}\}+0.6\exp\{-\left(6t/T_{1}\right)^{\beta_{\rm NMR}}\}, (6)

assuming that only the central transition was saturated while the populations of satellite transitions remain unaffected. The stretching exponent βNMR\beta_{\rm NMR} is indicative of a spatial distribution of T1T_{1} values. The temperature dependence of the extracted 1/T11/T_{1} and β\beta values is summarized in Figure 5 in the main text..
